parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 10. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman from a job agency giving information to a man about working for a chain of holiday parks. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Tessa: So, Callum, I understand you're interested in seasonal work this summer. Callum: That's right. I've just finished my second year at university, and I'd like to work somewhere outdoors if possible. Tessa: Have you done this kind of work before? Callum: A little. Last summer I worked at a sports centre, helping with children's holiday courses. I really enjoyed it, and I'd like to do something similar again. Tessa: That's useful experience. Employers in this area are always looking for people who are good with children. Tessa: Well, one company we work with is Greenway Holiday Parks. They have six parks around the coast, and they're a really good employer. There are quite a few benefits. Callum: Oh, good. What kind of benefits? Tessa: Well, first of all, all staff get free meals in the staff canteen, including seasonal workers like you. That's quite unusual in this industry. Callum: That would certainly help. Is accommodation included too? Tessa: Only for managers, I'm afraid, so you'd need to find your own. But another benefit is that staff can get a discount on holidays at any of the company's parks, for themselves and their families. The only time you can't use it is in August, because that's their busiest month. Callum: Fair enough. Are the parks easy to get to? I don't have a car. Tessa: Most of them are a few miles outside town, but the company runs a free minibus from the railway station for staff at the start and end of every shift. Callum: That's great. I was worried I'd have to cycle every day. Tessa: Now, they're quite specific about the kind of person they're looking for. They want people who can work well in a team, because everyone has to help each other out when it's busy. Callum: That's fine. I played in a football team for years, so I'm used to that. Tessa: They also like staff to be friendly and approachable, because guests often ask them for advice about things to do in the area. Callum: I'm happy to chat to people. I actually grew up near the coast, so I know quite a lot of places to recommend. Tessa: Good. And they also say that staff must take the safety of guests very seriously. A lot of their guests are families with young children, and many of the activities take place near water. Callum: Of course. That makes sense. Tessa: And finally, you must have a full driving licence, because staff sometimes have to drive the park vehicles. Callum: I've got one. I passed my test last year, although I haven't had much practice since. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Tessa: OK, let's look at the current vacancies. The first one is at their park at Penhallow Bay. Callum: Sorry, where? Tessa: Penhallow. That's P, E, N, H, A, L, L, O, W. It's on the south coast, about twenty minutes from the station. Callum: OK. What's the job? Tessa: They need an activities assistant. You'd be running clubs for children, things like games and treasure hunts, and you'd also be responsible for checking that the canoes are safe before each session on the lake. Callum: That sounds fun. What's the pay like? Tessa: It's ten forty an hour, which is a bit more than most holiday parks pay, and you'd get paid weekly. Callum: That's better than I expected. What else is there? Tessa: There's also a job at their Riverside park, as a reception assistant. You'd be checking guests in and out, answering the phone, and dealing with complaints, which can be quite challenging in the summer. Callum: I can imagine. What's the salary for that one? Tessa: That's an annual salary of twenty-one thousand five hundred, but it's a permanent job, so it would continue after the summer. Callum: I'd have to think about that, as I'm going back to university in October. What are the hours like? Tessa: Reception is open until ten at night, so there's a lot of evening work, but you'd never have to work on a Sunday evening, as the reception closes early then. Callum: OK. I think the activities job sounds best for me, to be honest. Tessa: I thought you might say that. Shall I send them your CV? Callum: Yes, please. Tessa: Great. The season starts at the end of May, and there's a two-day training course for all new staff the week before. I'll let you know as soon as I hear anything back from them. Callum: Thanks very much for your help. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a man talking to members of the public about plans for a new country park on the site of an old airfield. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Adrian: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Adrian Cole, and I'm the project manager for the new country park that's planned on the site of the old Hollins airfield. I'd like to start by explaining why we chose this particular site. The airfield was built during the Second World War, and some of you may remember the old hangars, which were taken down several years ago. Adrian: The airfield hasn't been used for flying for over thirty years, and some of the land has been rented out for grazing. It's true that it's close to the railway station, which is certainly convenient for visitors, but that wasn't one of our main reasons. What mattered most to us was that the towns in this area have very little public green space, so many families have nowhere nearby to walk or play. And the other key factor was that the old grassland already supports some rare wildlife. Skylarks nest there every spring, for example, and there are several unusual wild flowers, so we're keen to protect that. Adrian: We've already had a lot of feedback on our plans. Some people have told us they'd like more car parking, and we're looking into that. But the response has been very positive overall. People particularly liked the way the design protects the wildlife on the site, with quiet areas where visitors won't be allowed to go during the nesting season. And many people have told us that they're pleased the park will bring the community together, through volunteering days and events for local schools and clubs. Adrian: Entry to the park will be free, although there'll be a small charge for parking, which some people weren't so happy about. Adrian: We're hoping to open the first part of the park next spring, and the rest the following year. We'll also be looking for volunteers to help with tree planting and wildlife surveys, so if you're interested, please leave your details at the desk on your way out. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Adrian: Right, I'll put a map of the park up on the screen. You can see that the main road runs along the southern edge, and Mill Lane forms the western boundary. There are two entrances, one from the main road at the bottom of the map, and one from Mill Lane on the left. Adrian: From the south entrance, the main path goes straight up through the park. The first turning on the left goes to the car park, and the second turning on the left goes across to the west entrance. The visitor centre will be on the main path, on your left just before you reach the second turning. Adrian: If people arrive by bike, or want to hire one, the cycle hire will be on the western side of the park, just below the path that comes in from Mill Lane. Adrian: Now, at the top of the map, you can see the lake. Birdwatchers will be pleased to hear that we're building a bird hide on the western shore of the lake, at the end nearest to Mill Lane. Adrian: Over on the eastern side of the park is the old control tower from the airfield. We're keeping it, and the cafe will be built right next to it, on its north side, between the tower and the woodland. Adrian: There'll be a picnic area between the two entrances, near Mill Lane. You'll see three large oak trees on the map, and the picnic area will be just to the south of those. Adrian: And finally, the playground. If you follow the main path north from the south entrance, you'll see that at the top it curves round to the left towards the lake. The playground will be inside that curve, so parents will be able to watch their children and enjoy the views of the lake at the same time. OK, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two physics students, Rory and Leah, talking about a solar storm which took place in 1859. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Rory: So, Leah, shall we start planning our presentation on the Carrington Event? Leah: Yes, let's. I really enjoyed the reading. I'd never heard of it before this course. Rory: Me neither. It's often described as the biggest solar storm ever recorded, but apparently some scientists think there may have been even bigger ones in the distant past. Leah: That's true. But for me, that's not really why it matters. What makes it so important is that it was the first time a solar storm affected modern technology, the telegraph. It showed how vulnerable our systems could be. Rory: I agree. That should be the focus of our presentation. Leah: We could also talk about what would happen if a storm like that hit us today. Satellites, power grids, mobile phone networks. It could be a disaster. Rory: Yes. There was a much smaller storm in 1989 that caused a power cut across a large part of Canada for several hours. That would make a good comparison. Rory: Maybe we should start by explaining what a solar flare actually is, because some of the audience might not know. Leah: Good idea. We could say it's a sudden burst of energy from the surface of the sun, and that it's often followed by a huge cloud of charged particles that travels out into space. Rory: And when that cloud reaches Earth, it disturbs the planet's magnetic field. That's what causes the auroras, and the problems with electrical equipment. Leah: Exactly. We'll need a simple diagram for that. Leah: I was amazed by how many written records there are from the time. Rory: Me too. What surprised me most was that the observations came from so many different places, from ships at sea, from observatories, from ordinary people all over the world. They didn't always describe things in the same way, but the accounts fit together quite well. Leah: The descriptions of the aurora are fascinating. In some places, it was such a deep red that people thought a big fire had broken out nearby, and they called out the fire brigade. Rory: Imagine that. And it lasted for hours, not just a few minutes. Leah: Of course, Richard Carrington was the only astronomer who actually saw the solar flare that caused it all. That's why the event's named after him. Rory: Actually, that's not quite right. Another astronomer, Richard Hodgson, saw it at the same time from his own observatory, and they both reported it independently. Carrington just published first. Leah: Oh, I didn't know that. We should mention it. Rory: Yes, it seems a bit unfair that hardly anyone has heard of Hodgson. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Rory: What really surprised me was how far south the auroras were seen. Normally, you'd only expect them near the Arctic, but in 1859 they were visible in the Caribbean. Leah: I know. And they were so bright that people in some places could read a newspaper outside in the middle of the night. I'd never have imagined that. Rory: No. I wasn't surprised that the storm reached Earth so quickly, though. I knew that could happen. And luckily, nobody seems to have died as a direct result. Leah: That's true. Let's go through what happened in different countries. We could start with Britain, where Carrington was working. Rory: Yes. That's where the solar flare itself was observed, through a telescope, just before midday. Leah: Then the United States. My favourite story is the gold miners in the Rocky Mountains, who woke up in the middle of the night and started making breakfast, because it was so bright that they thought it was already morning. Rory: Ha, yes. Then there's Cuba, where people saw the aurora almost directly overhead, which is incredible for somewhere so close to the equator. Leah: And in France, the whole telegraph network was badly disrupted. Operators couldn't send messages for hours. Rory: Right. That gives us a good range of examples. Shall we start on the slides? I'll look for some pictures and old newspaper reports we could use, if you can start on the part about modern technology. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student on a design course giving a talk about the history of the umbrella. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Good morning. For this assignment, we were asked to choose an everyday object and look at how it has developed over time. I chose the umbrella. Almost everyone owns one, but because they're cheap and often disposable, we rarely think about them. When we lose one on a bus, we just buy another. Yet the umbrella has a surprisingly interesting history. Student: Umbrellas were used thousands of years ago in ancient Egypt, China and Persia. But in these hot countries they weren't used for rain at all. They were used for protection from the sun, and they were often a sign of high status. The word umbrella itself comes from the Latin word for shade. Student: In eighteenth-century Britain, umbrellas were used by women, but for a man to carry one was considered a sign of weakness. A gentleman was expected to put up with the rain, or to travel by coach. This began to change thanks to a man called Jonas Hanway, who is said to have carried an umbrella in the streets of London for about thirty years. At first, people laughed at him, and he faced particularly strong opposition from coachmen, who saw umbrellas as a threat to their business. After all, if people could stay dry while walking, they wouldn't need to hire a coach. Hanway was a merchant who had travelled widely, and he had seen umbrellas being used in other countries before he brought the habit back to London. Student: Early umbrellas were heavy and awkward. Their frames were made of whalebone or wood, and they were covered with canvas that had been treated with oil to make it waterproof. A wet umbrella could weigh several kilograms, and it often leaked. Student: The great breakthrough came in 1852, when a manufacturer called Samuel Fox designed a frame made of steel. Interestingly, the steel he used was left over from the production of corsets, the tight garments that women wore under their dresses at the time. Steel frames were much lighter and stronger, and the basic design Fox developed is still used in most umbrellas today. Umbrella shops became common in British cities, and one London shop that opened in the nineteenth century is still selling umbrellas today, in the same building. Student: In the twentieth century, the umbrella became an important part of men's fashion. In London, businessmen carried tightly rolled black umbrellas as a symbol of respectability, even on sunny days, and the umbrella became almost a part of the uniform of the city worker. Student: Then, in 1928, a German engineer invented the folding pocket umbrella. He had been injured in the First World War and needed to walk with a stick, so he wanted an umbrella that was small enough to carry easily at the same time as his walking stick. His design was a great success, and folding umbrellas soon became popular all over Europe, especially with people who travelled to work by train. Student: Today, umbrellas are produced in enormous numbers, and many are used for only a short time. Millions are thrown away every year, and because they're made of several materials, such as metal, plastic and fabric, all joined together, they're very difficult to recycle. Some designers are now trying to create umbrellas that can be easily taken apart, and I'll look at some of their ideas in the second part of my talk. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

The airfield was built during the Second World War, and some of you may remember the old hangars, which were taken down several years ago. Adrian: The airfield hasn't been used for flying for over thirty years, and some of the land has been rented out for grazing. It's true that it's close to the railway station, which is certainly convenient for visitors, but that wasn't one of our main reasons. What mattered most to us was that the towns in this area have very little public green space, so many families have nowhere nearby to walk or play. And the other key factor was that the old grassland already supports some rare wildlife. Skylarks nest there every spring, for example, and there are several unusual wild flowers, so we're keen to protect that. Adrian: We've already had a lot of feedback on our plans. Some people have told us they'd like more car parking, and we're looking into that. But the response has been very positive overall. People particularly liked the way the design protects the wildlife on the site, with quiet areas where visitors won't be allowed to go during the nesting season. And many people have told us that they're pleased the park will bring the community together, through volunteering days and events for local schools and clubs. Adrian: Entry to the park will be free, although there'll be a small charge for parking, which some people weren't so happy about. Adrian: We're hoping to open the first part of the park next spring, and the rest the following year. We'll also be looking for volunteers to help with tree planting and wildlife surveys, so if you're interested, please leave your details at the desk on your way out. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Adrian: Right, I'll put a map of the park up on the screen. You can see that the main road runs along the southern edge, and Mill Lane forms the western boundary. There are two entrances, one from the main road at the bottom of the map, and one from Mill Lane on the left. Adrian: From the south entrance, the main path goes straight up through the park. The first turning on the left goes to the car park, and the second turning on the left goes across to the west entrance. The visitor centre will be on the main path, on your left just before you reach the second turning. Adrian: If people arrive by bike, or want to hire one, the cycle hire will be on the western side of the park, just below the path that comes in from Mill Lane. Adrian: Now, at the top of the map, you can see the lake. Birdwatchers will be pleased to hear that we're building a bird hide on the western shore of the lake, at the end nearest to Mill Lane. Adrian: Over on the eastern side of the park is the old control tower from the airfield. We're keeping it, and the cafe will be built right next to it, on its north side, between the tower and the woodland. Adrian: There'll be a picnic area between the two entrances, near Mill Lane. You'll see three large oak trees on the map, and the picnic area will be just to the south of those. Adrian: And finally, the playground. If you follow the main path north from the south entrance, you'll see that at the top it curves round to the left towards the lake. The playground will be inside that curve, so parents will be able to watch their children and enjoy the views of the lake at the same time. OK, does anyone have any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two physics students, Rory and Leah, talking about a solar storm which took place in 1859. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Rory: So, Leah, shall we start planning our presentation on the Carrington Event? Leah: Yes, let's. I really enjoyed the reading. I'd never heard of it before this course. Rory: Me neither. It's often described as the biggest solar storm ever recorded, but apparently some scientists think there may have been even bigger ones in the distant past. Leah: That's true. But for me, that's not really why it matters. What makes it so important is that it was the first time a solar storm affected modern technology, the telegraph. It showed how vulnerable our systems could be. Rory: I agree. That should be the focus of our presentation. Leah: We could also talk about what would happen if a storm like that hit us today. Satellites, power grids, mobile phone networks. It could be a disaster. Rory: Yes. There was a much smaller storm in 1989 that caused a power cut across a large part of Canada for several hours. That would make a good comparison. Rory: Maybe we should start by explaining what a solar flare actually is, because some of the audience might not know. Leah: Good idea. We could say it's a sudden burst of energy from the surface of the sun, and that it's often followed by a huge cloud of charged particles that travels out into space. Rory: And when that cloud reaches Earth, it disturbs the planet's magnetic field. That's what causes the auroras, and the problems with electrical equipment. Leah: Exactly. We'll need a simple diagram for that. Leah: I was amazed by how many written records there are from the time. Rory: Me too. What surprised me most was that the observations came from so many different places, from ships at sea, from observatories, from ordinary people all over the world. They didn't always describe things in the same way, but the accounts fit together quite well. Leah: The descriptions of the aurora are fascinating. In some places, it was such a deep red that people thought a big fire had broken out nearby, and they called out the fire brigade. Rory: Imagine that. And it lasted for hours, not just a few minutes. Leah: Of course, Richard Carrington was the only astronomer who actually saw the solar flare that caused it all. That's why the event's named after him. Rory: Actually, that's not quite right. Another astronomer, Richard Hodgson, saw it at the same time from his own observatory, and they both reported it independently. Carrington just published first. Leah: Oh, I didn't know that. We should mention it. Rory: Yes, it seems a bit unfair that hardly anyone has heard of Hodgson. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Rory: What really surprised me was how far south the auroras were seen. Normally, you'd only expect them near the Arctic, but in 1859 they were visible in the Caribbean. Leah: I know. And they were so bright that people in some places could read a newspaper outside in the middle of the night. I'd never have imagined that. Rory: No. I wasn't surprised that the storm reached Earth so quickly, though. I knew that could happen. And luckily, nobody seems to have died as a direct result. Leah: That's true. Let's go through what happened in different countries. We could start with Britain, where Carrington was working. Rory: Yes. That's where the solar flare itself was observed, through a telescope, just before midday. Leah: Then the United States. My favourite story is the gold miners in the Rocky Mountains, who woke up in the middle of the night and started making breakfast, because it was so bright that they thought it was already morning. Rory: Ha, yes. Then there's Cuba, where people saw the aurora almost directly overhead, which is incredible for somewhere so close to the equator. Leah: And in France, the whole telegraph network was badly disrupted. Operators couldn't send messages for hours. Rory: Right. That gives us a good range of examples. Shall we start on the slides? I'll look for some pictures and old newspaper reports we could use, if you can start on the part about modern technology. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student on a design course giving a talk about the history of the umbrella. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Good morning. For this assignment, we were asked to choose an everyday object and look at how it has developed over time. I chose the umbrella. Almost everyone owns one, but because they're cheap and often disposable, we rarely think about them. When we lose one on a bus, we just buy another. Yet the umbrella has a surprisingly interesting history. Student: Umbrellas were used thousands of years ago in ancient Egypt, China and Persia. But in these hot countries they weren't used for rain at all. They were used for protection from the sun, and they were often a sign of high status. The word umbrella itself comes from the Latin word for shade. Student: In eighteenth-century Britain, umbrellas were used by women, but for a man to carry one was considered a sign of weakness. A gentleman was expected to put up with the rain, or to travel by coach. This began to change thanks to a man called Jonas Hanway, who is said to have carried an umbrella in the streets of London for about thirty years. At first, people laughed at him, and he faced particularly strong opposition from coachmen, who saw umbrellas as a threat to their business. After all, if people could stay dry while walking, they wouldn't need to hire a coach. Hanway was a merchant who had travelled widely, and he had seen umbrellas being used in other countries before he brought the habit back to London. Student: Early umbrellas were heavy and awkward. Their frames were made of whalebone or wood, and they were covered with canvas that had been treated with oil to make it waterproof. A wet umbrella could weigh several kilograms, and it often leaked. Student: The great breakthrough came in 1852, when a manufacturer called Samuel Fox designed a frame made of steel. Interestingly, the steel he used was left over from the production of corsets, the tight garments that women wore under their dresses at the time. Steel frames were much lighter and stronger, and the basic design Fox developed is still used in most umbrellas today. Umbrella shops became common in British cities, and one London shop that opened in the nineteenth century is still selling umbrellas today, in the same building. Student: In the twentieth century, the umbrella became an important part of men's fashion. In London, businessmen carried tightly rolled black umbrellas as a symbol of respectability, even on sunny days, and the umbrella became almost a part of the uniform of the city worker. Student: Then, in 1928, a German engineer invented the folding pocket umbrella. He had been injured in the First World War and needed to walk with a stick, so he wanted an umbrella that was small enough to carry easily at the same time as his walking stick. His design was a great success, and folding umbrellas soon became popular all over Europe, especially with people who travelled to work by train. Student: Today, umbrellas are produced in enormous numbers, and many are used for only a short time. Millions are thrown away every year, and because they're made of several materials, such as metal, plastic and fabric, all joined together, they're very difficult to recycle. Some designers are now trying to create umbrellas that can be easily taken apart, and I'll look at some of their ideas in the second part of my talk. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
